theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: You are about to start a plant round to take readings. What should you do first?
options: Start with the gauges nearest the door to save time
Find out which readings are needed and their normal range
Tap each gauge hard so that the pointer settles quickly
Ask the operator to stop the plant so all gauges read zero

questions.stem: Where should you look to find the normal working pressure of a pump on the line?
options: On the price label on the box the gauge came in
In the Centre's fire drill notice on the wall
In the cleaning schedule for the plant room
In the maker's manual or the plant's log sheet

questions.stem: Why should you know the expected reading before you take a measurement?
options: So that you can spot a reading that is wrong or unsafe
So that you can write it down without taking a reading
So that you can turn the pointer to show that value
So that you do not need to note the units used

The store clerk who gave out the test gauge
The supervisor or the person in charge of the plant
Nobody's permission, as long as you work quickly

questions.stem: Which PPE is most needed when taking readings beside hot water and steam pipes?

Safety glasses and gloves suited to hot surfaces
A high-visibility vest only, so others see you

questions.stem: You find a pressure gauge with a cracked glass face and a bent pointer. What should you do?

Straighten the pointer with pliers and carry on

Tag it as faulty and report it for replacement

questions.stem: What is the safe order for taking a pressure gauge off a line?

Unscrew it slowly, then close its isolating valve once fluid starts to leak out
Vent the pressure, unscrew it, then close its isolating valve to stop the flow

questions.stem: You will measure a motor's shaft speed with an optical (light-beam) tachometer. When should the reflective tape be stuck on the shaft?

At any time, as long as you are wearing gloves
While the motor is stopped and isolated
After the reading, so the tape can be checked

questions.stem: Why must loose clothing, long hair and jewellery be secured when taking readings near running machines?

They can be caught by moving parts and pull you in

questions.stem: Which fault on a meter's test leads means they must not be used?

One lead is red and the other lead is black

questions.stem: A pump normally runs at about 400 kPa. Which pressure gauge range is the best choice?

0 to 800 kPa

questions.stem: Which instrument measures the surface temperature of a part without touching it?

questions.stem: Which instrument is used to measure the speed of a turning shaft?

questions.stem: To avoid parallax error when reading a dial gauge, how should you look at it?
options: From a little to one side of the pointer
From below, looking up at the dial
With your eye square on to the pointer

10 kPa

Accurate but not repeatable
Neither accurate nor repeatable
Repeatable but not accurate

questions.stem: What is a 'zero check' on a gauge or meter?
options: Checking that there are no scratches on the face
Checking that the battery is fully charged

Checking that nobody has used it that day

The lowest range, then step up
Any range, as the meter will not mind

questions.stem: What is a thermowell?

A box on the wall where thermometers are kept

questions.stem: An infrared thermometer is most likely to give a wrong reading on which surface?

A coloured liquid in a thin glass tube rises as it warms
A strip made of two metals bends and moves a pointer
Two unlike metals joined at a tip make a small voltage

questions.stem: What makes a resistance temperature detector (RTD) work?
options: Its outside colour changes as it heats up
Its resistance changes with temperature
It gives off more infrared light as it warms
It makes a small voltage where two metals meet

questions.stem: Why should you wait a short time before reading a probe thermometer that has just been put into hot water?

So the display can change to °F

questions.stem: What is a sight glass on a tank used for?

questions.stem: In which units is the flow of water in a pipe usually given?

questions.stem: A clamp meter's jaws are closed around a whole two-core flexible cord, with both wires inside the jaws. What will it read?
options: About twice the real load current
About zero, as the two currents cancel
Exactly the real load current, as normal
The supply voltage, not the current

questions.stem: How is an ammeter (not a clamp type) connected to measure current?
options: Across the supply, the same way as a voltmeter
Between the line conductor and earth
Held near the cable, with no connection made
In series, so the current flows through it

questions.stem: Before you measure the resistance of a heater element that is wired into a circuit, the circuit must be:
options: isolated and proved dead
switched on so current flows
connected to the earth bar
running at its full load

questions.stem: What does the measurement category (CAT) rating printed on a meter tell you?
options: The colour code used for its test leads
How many readings it can save in its memory
Where in a supply system it is safe to use
Which size of battery the meter needs to work

questions.stem: Many transmitters send a 4–20 mA signal. Why does the signal start at 4 mA and not at 0 mA?
options: So that the signal wire uses less power from the supply
So a broken wire can be told apart from a zero reading
So the meter needle never hits its end stop pin hard
So the signal can be read on an ordinary voltmeter

questions.stem: How often should a measuring instrument be calibrated?
options: Only once, when it is first bought
Only after it has been dropped
Before every single reading taken
At the interval in the schedule

questions.stem: The calibration label on a gauge shows that its due date has passed. What should you do?
options: Tag it out of use and send it for calibration
Use it, but add a note saying it may be wrong
Use it for one more month, then report it
Peel the label off so that nobody is confused

questions.stem: A test gauge has been dropped on a concrete floor. What should be done before it is used again?
options: Shake it gently to settle the pointer back down
Clean the face so the reading can be seen well
Have it checked against a known good gauge
Nothing, as long as the glass did not break

questions.stem: How should a digital meter be stored after use?
options: Left switched on so the battery stays charged
Switched off, in its case, in a cool dry place
On the window sill so it stays dry in the sun
In a toolbox under heavy spanners and hammers

questions.stem: As well as the number, what should you write for each reading on a log sheet?
options: The weather, the shift team and the gauge colour
The gauge's price, its maker and how old it is
The tools you used and the time of your next break

questions.stem: A reading is well outside its normal range. What should you do first?
options: Change the figure on the sheet to the normal value
Wait until the end of the shift to tell anyone
Check it, record it and tell the supervisor at once

essays.stem: Describe the main hazards when taking instrument readings in a plant room, and say how you would control each one.
essays.modelAnswer: A plant room has several hazards. Hot pipes, steam lines and tanks can burn, so I wear gloves suited to heat, keep my sleeves down and never touch a line before checking it. Pressurised lines can leak or burst, so I never loosen a fitting or remove a gauge while it is under pressure, and I wear safety glasses. Running machines have shafts, belts and couplings that can catch clothing, hair or jewellery, so I tie these back, keep guards in place and never reach past a guard. Electrical panels can give a shock, so I do not open them, and I only use meters and leads that are in good condition and have the right CAT rating. Noise can damage hearing, so I wear ear protection where the signs say so. Wet or oily floors cause slips, so I wear safety boots and report spills. I follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules, and I tell the supervisor where I am working.
markingPoints: Hot surfaces and steam: heat-resistant gloves, sleeves down, do not touch before checking
Pressure: never loosen fittings or remove gauges under pressure; safety glasses
Moving parts: secure clothing, hair and jewellery; guards stay on
Electrical: do not open panels; leads and meter in good condition with a suitable CAT rating
Noise and slips: ear protection, safety boots, report spills; follow the Centre's rules

essays.stem: Explain how you would choose the right instrument to make a measurement on the job.
essays.modelAnswer: First I decide what I must measure, such as pressure, temperature, flow, level, speed or an electrical value, and which units are needed. Next I find the expected value and choose an instrument whose range covers it with room to spare, so that the normal reading sits near the middle of the scale and the instrument cannot be over-ranged. I check that its accuracy and resolution are good enough for the job, for example whether I need readings to 1 °C or to 0.1 °C. I think about the conditions: heat, water, dust, vibration, or a moving or hot part that I cannot safely touch, where a non-contact instrument such as an infrared thermometer or an optical tachometer is better. For electrical measurements the meter must have a suitable CAT rating. Finally I check that the instrument is in date for calibration, clean, undamaged and working, and I read the maker's instructions before I use it.
markingPoints: Identify the quantity to be measured and the units needed
Range covers the expected value with the normal reading near mid-scale (not over-ranged)
Accuracy and resolution good enough for the job
Suits the conditions: contact or non-contact, heat, water, moving parts, CAT rating
Checked before use: in date for calibration, undamaged, maker's instructions read

essays.stem: Describe how you would fit a test pressure gauge to a test point on a line and take a reading safely.
essays.modelAnswer: I get permission from the supervisor and tell the operator what I am doing. I check the test gauge: its range suits the line pressure, its calibration label is in date, the glass and pointer are not damaged, and its thread matches the test point. I wear safety glasses and gloves. With the test point's isolating valve closed, I open the vent slowly to make sure no pressure is trapped. I screw the gauge on using a spanner on the gauge's square or hex, not by twisting the case, and hold the fitting with a second spanner. I use thread tape or a seal where needed. I stand to one side and open the isolating valve slowly so the pointer does not jump, then check for leaks. I let the pointer settle, read it square on, and record the reading with its units, the time and my initials. When I have finished, I close the valve and vent the pressure before the gauge is taken off.
markingPoints: Permission obtained and the operator told
Test gauge checked: suitable range, calibration in date, no damage, correct thread
Fitted with the right tools on the gauge's hex (not the case), sealed, PPE worn
Valve opened slowly, leaks checked, standing to one side
Reading taken square on after settling and recorded with units, time and initials

essays.stem: Explain what 'accuracy', 'repeatability' and 'calibration' mean, and why measuring instruments must be calibrated.
essays.modelAnswer: Accuracy means how close a reading is to the true value. Repeatability means how close the readings are to each other when the same thing is measured several times. An instrument can be repeatable but still not accurate, for example a gauge that always reads 20 kPa low. Calibration means comparing the instrument with a standard that is known to be more accurate, recording the errors at several points across its range, and adjusting or correcting it if the errors are too big. A label then shows the date it was checked and when it is next due. Instruments drift over time, and they can be damaged by knocks, drops, heat, over-pressure or over-range. If an instrument is wrong, a plant may be run at an unsafe pressure or temperature, products may be spoiled and faults can be missed. Calibration keeps readings trustworthy, and an instrument that is out of date or damaged is tagged out of use.
markingPoints: Accuracy: how close the reading is to the true value
Repeatability: how close repeated readings are to each other (with an example)
Calibration: compare with a more accurate standard, record errors, adjust, label with due date
Why: instruments drift or are damaged; wrong readings can be unsafe or costly
Out-of-date or damaged instruments are tagged out of use

essays.stem: Compare a thermocouple, a resistance temperature detector (RTD) and an infrared thermometer. Say how each one works and give one good use for each.
essays.modelAnswer: A thermocouple is made of two different metals joined at the tip. When the tip is heated, a small voltage is made, and the instrument turns this voltage into a temperature. Thermocouples are tough and cheap and cover a wide range, so they suit high temperatures such as ovens, furnaces and engine exhausts. An RTD has a fine metal element, often platinum, whose resistance rises as it gets hotter. It is more accurate and steady than a thermocouple, over a smaller range, so it suits process pipes and tanks where close control is needed. An infrared thermometer does not touch the surface; it measures the infrared heat given off by the surface. It is quick, and safe for moving, hard-to-reach or hot parts, such as checking a motor casing or a bearing housing. It can read wrongly on shiny surfaces, and it only measures the surface, not the inside of the part.
markingPoints: Thermocouple: two different metals make a small voltage; use such as ovens or high temperatures
RTD: resistance of a metal element changes with temperature; accurate, for process pipes or tanks
Infrared: non-contact, measures heat given off; for moving, hot or hard-to-reach parts
A sensible comparison: range, accuracy, contact or non-contact
A limitation, such as shiny surfaces or surface-only readings for infrared

essays.stem: Describe how you would carry out a plant round, taking and recording readings on a log sheet.
essays.modelAnswer: Before starting I collect the log sheet and check the list of points to read and the normal range for each one. I tell the supervisor and the operator that I am doing the round, and I wear the PPE needed. I check that my own instruments, such as a thermometer or tachometer, are working and in date for calibration. At each point I stand in a safe place, look at the gauge square on and wait for the pointer or display to settle. I write the reading straight away, with its units, the time and my initials, and compare it with the normal range. If a reading looks odd I check it again, and if I can, with a second instrument. I never change a reading, and I do not adjust plant controls that I am not allowed to touch. Any reading outside the range, and any leak, strange noise, smell or damaged gauge, is reported to the supervisor at once. At the end I hand in the completed, signed log sheet.
markingPoints: Prepares: log sheet, normal ranges, tells the supervisor and operator, PPE, instruments checked
Reads safely and correctly: safe position, square on, waits for the reading to settle
Records at once with units, time and initials; never alters a reading
Compares with the normal range and re-checks odd readings
Reports abnormal readings or plant problems at once; hands in the signed sheet

essays.stem: Explain how you would use a meter safely to measure the resistance of a heater element in a piece of equipment.
essays.modelAnswer: Resistance must only be measured on a dead circuit, because the meter sends its own small current through the part, and a live supply can damage the meter or injure me. First I isolate the supply: switch off, lock off and tag, then prove dead with a voltage tester that I check on a known live source or a proving unit before and after the test. I disconnect at least one end of the element, so that other parts of the circuit do not give a false reading. I inspect the meter and leads for damage, set the meter to the resistance (ohms) range, and touch the probes together to check it reads near zero. Then I hold the probes firmly on the element's terminals, with my fingers behind the finger guards, and read the value once it is steady. I compare it with the maker's figure: a very high reading means the element is broken. I record the result and keep the circuit locked off until the work is finished.
markingPoints: States resistance is measured only on a dead circuit, and why
Safe isolation: switch off, lock off, tag, prove dead with a tester checked before and after
Disconnects one end of the element to avoid false readings
Checks meter and leads, sets the ohms range, does a lead (zero) check
Takes a steady reading, compares it with the maker's figure and records it

essays.stem: Describe how measuring instruments should be handled, cared for and stored so that they stay accurate.
essays.modelAnswer: Instruments are delicate and must be treated with care. I carry them in their cases, never drop or throw them, and do not leave them where they can be knocked or stood on. I keep them away from heat, direct sun, water and dust, and I wipe them clean with a dry cloth after use. Pressure gauges must never be used above their range, and I open valves slowly so that the pointer does not slam against its stop. Meters are switched off after use, and the battery is taken out if the meter will not be used for a long time, so that it cannot leak. Test leads are coiled loosely, not wrapped tightly round the meter. Before use I check each instrument for damage and for an in-date calibration label. If an instrument is dropped, damaged or gives odd readings, I tag it out of use and report it so it can be checked. Instruments are signed out and back in so they can be traced.
markingPoints: Handled gently and carried and stored in their cases
Kept away from heat, sun, water and dust, and cleaned after use
Not over-ranged; valves opened slowly
Switched off after use; batteries removed for long storage; leads coiled loosely
Checked before use; damaged or doubtful instruments tagged and reported; signed in and out

essays.stem: Explain how a comparison check of a workshop pressure gauge against a reference gauge is done, and how you decide whether the workshop gauge can stay in use.
essays.modelAnswer: I get a reference gauge that is in date for calibration and more accurate than the workshop gauge, and a test rig fed from a regulated supply. Both gauges are fitted to the same manifold so that they see the same pressure. I check that all fittings are tight, that the supply is set low to start, and I wear safety glasses. I raise the pressure in steps, for example at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 % of the workshop gauge's scale. At each step I let the pointers settle and record both readings. Then I lower the pressure in the same steps and record again, because some gauges read differently going up and coming down. For each point I work out the error: the workshop reading minus the reference reading. If every error is within the tolerance given by the maker or the Centre, the gauge passes and is labelled. If not, it is tagged out of use and sent for adjustment or replacement. Finally I vent the pressure before taking the gauges off.
markingPoints: Uses an in-date, more accurate reference gauge on the same manifold, regulated supply, PPE
Raises the pressure in steps across the scale and records both readings at each step
Repeats with falling pressure
Works out the error at each point (workshop minus reference)
Compares with the tolerance: pass and label, or tag out of use; vents before removal

essays.stem: Explain how a 4–20 mA signal from a transmitter shows a reading. Then work out the pressure shown by a 0 to 1 000 kPa pressure transmitter that is sending 8 mA. Show your working.
essays.modelAnswer: A transmitter turns the measured value into a small current. A current of 4 mA means the bottom of the range (0 %), and 20 mA means the top of the range (100 %). So the span of the signal is 20 − 4 = 16 mA. To find the reading, take 4 mA away from the current, divide by 16, and multiply by the range: value = (current − 4) ÷ 16 × range. A current signal is used because it is not changed by the length or resistance of the signal wires. For the 0 to 1 000 kPa transmitter sending 8 mA: 8 − 4 = 4 mA above the bottom of the range. 4 ÷ 16 = 0.25, which is 25 % of the range. 25 % of 1 000 kPa is 0.25 × 1 000 = 250 kPa. So the pressure is 250 kPa. I would check that the local gauge or display agrees with this value.
markingPoints: 4 mA = 0 % (bottom of range) and 20 mA = 100 % (top of range)
Span of 16 mA and the method: (current − 4) ÷ 16 × range
Correct answer: 250 kPa
A reason for using current (not changed by wire length) or checking against a local display

practical1.title: Plant round: measure and record pressure, temperature, speed and resistance
practical1.brief: As a group, carry out a plant round at four measuring stations that the assessor sets up, and record every reading on the group's log sheet. Station 1: read the receiver pressure gauge on the Centre's air compressor (or pressure rig) every 15 minutes. Station 2: measure the temperature of hot water in an insulated container with a probe thermometer, and with an infrared thermometer aimed at a matt, painted patch on the container, and compare the two. Station 3: measure the shaft speed of a guarded motor on the training bench with an optical tachometer; the instructor fits the reflective tape while the motor is stopped and isolated. Station 4: measure the resistance of three heater elements or resistors that are not connected to any supply. Each member leads one station and explains its instrument to the group, and every member takes at least one reading at every station. In a group of five, the fifth member keeps the log sheet and checks each entry, then swaps with a station leader halfway. Compare each reading with the normal range the assessor gives, and fill in a report form for any reading outside it. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the instruments are back in their cases.
materials: Air compressor or pressure rig with a dial gauge, set up and run by the instructor
Insulated container of hot water (not boiling), on a stable bench
Optical tachometer and reflective tape; motor on a guarded training bench
Meter with a resistance (ohms) range, and test leads in good condition
Three heater elements or resistors, not connected to any supply
Log sheet showing the normal ranges, and an abnormal-reading report form
photos: The four stations set up, with the instruments laid out
Each member taking a reading at their own station, eyes square to the scale
The probe and infrared thermometers in use on the hot water
The tachometer display showing the motor speed, with the guard in place
The meter display showing the resistance of one element
The completed log sheet, with units, times and initials
The report form for any reading outside its normal range
checklist: Checked each instrument before use: no damage, calibration label in date, zero or lead check done
Chose the right instrument and range for each measurement
Read each scale or display correctly, square on, after it had settled
Recorded every reading at once, with units, time and initials
Compared readings with the normal range and reported any reading outside it
Kept clear of moving parts and hot surfaces, and wore the PPE needed
Measured resistance only on parts with no supply connected
Explained their station's instrument clearly to the rest of the group
Cleaned the instruments and returned them to their cases
safety: Do not touch, loosen or remove any gauge or fitting on the compressor; only the instructor adjusts it
Keep hands, hair, sleeves and jewellery well clear of the running motor; the guard stays on
No boiling water; keep the hot water container on a stable bench and wear gloves to handle it
Do not open any electrical panel; measure resistance only on parts not connected to a supply
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules for every instrument

practical2.title: Comparison check of a pressure gauge and a thermometer
practical2.brief: As a group, check a workshop pressure gauge and a workshop thermometer against reference instruments, and complete a calibration check record for each. The instructor sets up a test manifold fed with regulated, low-pressure compressed air (kept below the lowest rating of any part on the rig), with the workshop gauge and an in-date reference gauge side by side. The group raises the pressure in five steps across the workshop gauge's scale and records both readings at each step, then lowers it in the same steps and records again. Next, check the workshop thermometer in a mix of crushed ice and water (0 °C), and then in warm water beside a reference thermometer. Work out the error at every point, decide whether each instrument passes against the tolerance the assessor gives, and fix a pass label or an out-of-use tag. Members take turns: one sets the regulator while the instructor watches, one reads the workshop gauge, one reads the reference gauge, one records and works out the errors, and one runs the thermometer check. Swap roles so that each member does at least two different jobs. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Test manifold with a pressure regulator, isolating valve and vent valve, set up by the instructor
Workshop pressure gauge and an in-date reference gauge
Workshop thermometer and an in-date reference thermometer
Insulated cup with crushed ice and clean water; a container of warm water
Calibration check record sheets and a calculator
photos: The test manifold with both gauges fitted and labelled
Both gauges at one test point, with both readings clearly visible
The vent valve open and both gauges at zero before anything is removed
The workshop thermometer in the ice-and-water mix
The workshop and reference thermometers together in warm water
The completed check records, with the errors worked out
Each instrument with its pass label or out-of-use tag
checklist: Wore safety glasses and checked the fittings were tight before pressure was applied
Raised and lowered the pressure in steady steps, without letting the pointer slam
Read both gauges correctly, square on, after the pointers settled
Recorded readings with units and worked out each error correctly (workshop minus reference)
Made the right pass or fail decision against the given tolerance
Set up the ice-and-water check correctly and waited for a steady reading
Vented the pressure and checked both gauges read zero before any fitting was loosened
Labelled or tagged each instrument and returned all the equipment
safety: Only the instructor connects the air supply; keep the pressure below the lowest rating on the rig
Never loosen a fitting until the pressure is vented and both gauges read zero
Never point compressed air at anyone or use it to blow dust off clothes or skin
Wear safety glasses throughout and stand to one side of the gauges, not in front of their faces
Wipe up spilled water at once so that nobody slips
